\section[\texorpdfstring{\ur{رفتار} (raftār)}{رفتار (raftār)}]{\ur{رفتار} (raftār) — speed}

\label{lesson:UR-C284-raftar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Urdu for a punishment, then the Urdu for handcuffs.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{رفتار}}
\textbf{\ur{رفتار}} — \emph{raftār} — \textquotedblleft{}speed\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ur{میں} \ur{کم} \ur{رفتار} \ur{سے} \ur{جاؤں} \ur{گا۔}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{maiṅ kam raftār se jāūṅ gā.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
I will go at a low speed.
\end{quote}

Feminine.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{رفتار}} (\emph{raftār}) is usually traced to Persian \emph{raftār}, \textquotedblleft{}a going, a gait\textquotedblright{}, from the Persian verb to go. It is feminine: \textbf{\ur{تیز} \ur{رفتار}}, high speed.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling what happened.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{raftār}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{raftār}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{maiṅ kam raftār se jāūṅ gā.} — I will go at a low speed.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Urdu for a punishment, then the Urdu for handcuffs, then say \emph{raftār} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ur{رفتار} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Speed\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\ur{ٹکرانا} (ṭakrānā)}{ٹکرانا (ṭakrānā)}]{\ur{ٹکرانا} (ṭakrānā) — to collide; to crash into}

\label{lesson:UR-C284-takrana}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Urdu for handcuffs, then the Urdu for speed.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{ٹکرانا}}
\textbf{\ur{ٹکرانا}} — \emph{ṭakrānā} — \textquotedblleft{}to collide; to crash into\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ur{بس} \ur{ایک} \ur{ٹرک} \ur{سے} \ur{ٹکرائی۔}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{bas ek ṭrak se ṭakrāī.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
The bus crashed into a lorry.
\end{quote}

Past (it …): \ur{وہ} \ur{گاڑی} \ur{ٹکرائی}, \emph{voh gāṛī ṭakrāī}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{ٹکرانا}} (\emph{ṭakrānā}) is built on \emph{ṭakkar}, \textquotedblleft{}a blow\textquotedblright{}, which CDIAL lists for Hindi under \emph{ṭakkarā} (CDIAL 5424). What you crash into takes \textbf{\ur{سے}}: \textbf{\ur{ٹرک} \ur{سے} \ur{ٹکرائی}}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling what happened.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ṭakrānā}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{bas ek ṭrak se ṭakrāī.} — The bus crashed into a lorry.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Urdu for handcuffs, then the Urdu for speed, then say \emph{ṭakrānā} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ur{ٹکرانا} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To collide; to crash into\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ur{پہیا} (pahiyā)}{پہیا (pahiyā)}]{\ur{پہیا} (pahiyā) — a wheel}

\label{lesson:UR-C284-pahiya}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Urdu for speed, then the Urdu for to collide.

Masculine.

\end{cousinweb}

One more word for telling what happened.

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ur{الٹنا} (ulaṭnā)}{الٹنا (ulaṭnā)}]{\ur{الٹنا} (ulaṭnā) — to overturn}

\label{lesson:UR-C284-ulatna}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Urdu for to collide, then the Urdu for a wheel.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{الٹنا}}
\textbf{\ur{الٹنا}} — \emph{ulaṭnā} — \textquotedblleft{}to overturn\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ur{ٹرک} \ur{سڑک} \ur{پر} \ur{الٹ} \ur{گیا۔}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{ṭrak saṛak par ulaṭ gayā.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
The lorry overturned on the road.
\end{quote}

Past (it …): \ur{وہ} \ur{ٹرک} \ur{الٹ} \ur{گیا}, \emph{voh ṭrak ulaṭ gayā}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{الٹنا}} (\emph{ulaṭnā}) is inherited: CDIAL lists the Hindi cousin \emph{ulaṭnā}, \textquotedblleft{}to be overturned\textquotedblright{}, under \emph{*ullaṭati}, a form it reconstructs (CDIAL 2368). A vehicle \textbf{\ur{الٹ} \ur{گئی}} when it lands on its side or its roof.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling what happened.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ur{سواری} (savārī)}{سواری (savārī)}]{\ur{سواری} (savārī) — a ride; a passenger}

\label{lesson:UR-C284-savari}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Urdu for a wheel, then the Urdu for to overturn.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{سواری}}
\textbf{\ur{سواری}} — \emph{savārī} — \textquotedblleft{}a ride; a passenger\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ur{بس} \ur{میں} \ur{بیس} \ur{سواریاں} \ur{تھیں۔}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{bas meṅ bīs savāriyāṅ thīṅ.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
There were twenty passengers on the bus.
\end{quote}

Feminine.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{سواری}} (\emph{savārī}) is usually traced to Persian \emph{savārī}, \textquotedblleft{}riding\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{savār}, a rider. It is feminine whoever the passenger is: \textbf{\ur{بیس} \ur{سواریاں}}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling what happened.
\end{grammarlens}
